title: Content-Security-Policy and Trusted Types
summary: The second layer: a strict CSP with a fresh nonce per response and 'strict-dynamic', so injected scripts do not run even when encoding is missed. Report-only roll-out, and Trusted Types against DOM XSS.

steps.title: A policy the browser enforces
body: `Content-Security-Policy` is a response header that tells the browser which scripts it may run. A **strict** policy, as Google's security team recommends it:

- **`'nonce-...'`**: a random value, **new for every response**, that the server puts both in the header and on its own `<script>` tags. An attacker who injects markup cannot know this response's nonce.

- **`'strict-dynamic'`**: a trusted script may load more scripts (bundlers, tag managers) and those are trusted too, so you do not have to list every CDN. Host lists like `script-src https://cdn.example` are weaker: any JSONP endpoint or old library on that host becomes a bypass.
- **`object-src 'none'`** (no plugins) and **`base-uri 'none'`** (no `<base href>` that redirects relative script URLs).

steps.prompt: With `script-src 'nonce-abc123' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'` on this response, does it run?
items: a script that `<script nonce="abc123">` adds with `document.createElement('script')`
`<script nonce="abc123">` copied from yesterday's page into a review today... on today's response with a new nonce
steps.explain: The nonce must change on every response; a fixed nonce is a password printed on every page. Inline event handlers and `javascript:` URLs never carry a nonce, so a strict policy blocks them all.

steps.title: Rolling it out without breaking the site
body: 1. Ship it as **`Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`** first, with a `report-to` (or the older `report-uri`) endpoint. Nothing is blocked; every violation is reported.
2. Fix what the reports show: move inline `onclick=` handlers into script files or nonced blocks (`addEventListener`), add the nonce to every `<script>` your templates write.
3. Switch the header name to `Content-Security-Policy`. Keep reporting on, so a regression shows up in your logs, not in a bug bounty.

Things that weaken a policy to watch for in review: `'unsafe-inline'` (ignored when a nonce is present in modern browsers, but a sign the nonce is missing somewhere), `'unsafe-eval'`, `*` or `https:` in `script-src`, and a nonce that is reused or predictable.

CSP is **defence in depth**. It turns most XSS bugs into blocked attempts in your reports. It does not replace encoding: data can still be stolen by injected markup without scripts (a fake login form, a dangling `

steps.prompt: A team generates one nonce when the app starts and reuses it for every response "for performance". What does that do to the policy?
options: It defeats it: an attacker reads the nonce from any page and puts it on their injected script
Nothing: the nonce is still random
steps.explain: A nonce works because the attacker cannot predict it when the injection is written. 16 random bytes from `RandomNumberGenerator` per response costs microseconds.

steps.title: Trusted Types: DOM XSS, stopped at the sink
body: DOM XSS happens in your own JavaScript: `el.innerHTML = untrusted`. **Trusted Types** make the browser refuse plain strings at those dangerous sinks:

Now the only way to write HTML into the page is through the policies you named, so a review only has to check those. Chromium-based browsers have enforced Trusted Types for years, and the other engines have been adding them; check current support for your users' browsers, and roll them out report-only first, like the rest of the CSP. Where a browser does not enforce them, the page still works, just without the extra check. The simplest fix for most sinks needs no policy: use `textContent` instead of `innerHTML`.

steps.prompt: Complete the strict policy the shop sends with every page.

steps.title: A nonce per response
prompt: Add a strict CSP to the shop's page:

1. A middleware (`app.Use(async (ctx, next) => { ... await next(); })`) that makes a nonce from **16 random bytes** (`RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(16)`, Base64), stores it in `ctx.Items["csp-nonce"]`, and sets the header:
2. The page's `<script>` gets `nonce="<nonce>"`, so it keeps running.
Add `using System.Security.Cryptography;` at the top. **Run checks** loads the page twice.
hints: In the page, read it back with `(string)ctx.Items["csp-nonce"]!` and make the raw string interpolated (`$"""`) so `{nonce}` is filled in.
template: public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
await Dojo.TryAsync("The page could be loaded", async () =>
var csp = r1.Headers.TryGetValues("Content-Security-Policy", out var v) ? string.Join(";", v) : "";
Dojo.Check("there is a Content-Security-Policy header", csp.Length > 0, "no header");
Dojo.Check("script-src has a nonce", m.Success, csp);
Dojo.Check("the nonce is 16 random bytes in Base64", raw.Length >= 16, nonce);
var csp2 = r2.Headers.TryGetValues("Content-Security-Policy", out var v2) ? string.Join(";", v2) : "";
Dojo.Check("every response gets a new nonce", csp2.Length > 0 && csp2 != csp, csp2);
Dojo.Check("the page's script carries this response's nonce", nonce.Length > 0 && page.Contains($"<script nonce=\"{nonce}\">"), page);
